cues.text: Mercy
I studied the word linguistically and showed that it combines sincere praise with unconditional gratitude. Both are owed to Allah because of his constant, relentless, never-ending over his .
The wording is not merely , but . Ultimate praise and absolute gratitude belong to him because he is .
Then he says : the abundantly merciful, the consistently merciful.
The word generally means mercy, but it points to a particular kind of mercy. It brings two things together in such a way that the principles of can apply.
For this reason, the womb of a mother is called . It brings the baby and the mother together so the mother can nurture the baby, pour her love over it, sustain the fetus, and help it grow.
The word is therefore so powerful that the ordinary English word “mercy” does not fully capture its essence.

In this next verse, Allah highlights His by giving a whole verse to the quality of His . According to Him, the essence and defining attribute of His is . It appears through His abundance, His , and through His consistency, His .

For this reason, when I look around and study the , I find one thread of running through the whole fabric of His . It is the glue that lovingly holds this together. It is like a magnetic force that naturally draws us toward Allah and keeps us connected with our Master.
In visual terms, His is like a gravitational field: a force of love that pulls us toward Him. What I experience from that pull is : ultimate praise and absolute gratitude owed to this , who is and .
Gratitude

I now turn to the gratitude within , to the aspect of . What is the reality of ? What is sincere gratitude when it becomes visible in a person? It is . It is constant awareness of Allah's presence. It is constant recognition and awareness of His blessings.
This is a very high station. It holds a lofty , and not everyone can truly reach the highest ranks of . This is why Allah says:

Very few of my servants are . The is not the same as the . The , the grateful one, gives thanks for Allah's blessings. The gives thanks even for calamities and trials, not only for blessings. He feels gratitude when painful things befall him.
Most people, at their best, are patient or resigned. The , however, says while he is living through those calamities, because he knows that Allah only does good for His believer. There is a hadith:

How wondrous is the affair of the believer; all of his affair is good. For the believer, all of it is good. When that belief becomes real, a person enters a state of constant gratitude, even for tribulations: .

The words of are always worth remembering: no matter how bad something is, it could always be worse. There are people who live like this. Even among non-Muslims, there are people who always look toward the good side: it could be worse; blessings can still be counted.
I find in this verse that Allah says he is a marked by and . His appears in our lives through his blessings, his gifts, and his . The abundance of his love becomes visible in what he gives.

As a parent, when I want to show love to my children, I do it by giving them gifts: valuable gifts, desirable gifts, beneficial gifts, gifts the child knows he or she could never have gained by personal effort alone. The blessings and gifts that Allah has bestowed upon us are astonishing gifts, infinite gifts.
If I attempted to enumerate the blessings of Allah, I would never be able to enumerate them. . These gifts are not only impossible to count; their value is impossible to measure.
I can take even one single , one of the eye, and the meaning becomes clear. This is only one .

The first example is blinking. I hardly notice that I blink at all. Yet when that small action is lost, its mercy becomes visible. Aristotle Onassis, one of the richest men in the world, owned a private fleet of ships. In old age, he had to use Band-Aids to hold up his eyelids because he lost the function of the muscle that lifts them back. His eyelids kept dropping, so he held them open.

Then he had to put drops in his eyes constantly, because eyelids that do not close leave the eyes dry and exposed to dust. Blinking does more than shut the eye. It works like a windshield wiper. It draws dust downward, moves it toward the sides, and gathers it in the corners. When I wipe my eyes, I may find a little dust there without ever thinking about the mercy that brought it there.

That is only one part of the eye. Beyond it lies the intricate network of its nerves, the myelination of the sheath, the constant synaptic response, and the neural transmission that allows sight to function. For some people, that system breaks down. I scarcely think about any of it.
I think of the electrical work involved in the eye's function.

I then turn to colors, to colors themselves. Allah could have made the whole world black and white. Instead, He placed in it subtle colors that the eye can receive and enjoy in astonishing variety. That, too, is .

Some colors give pleasure simply by being seen. The mind may not pause over them, yet they carry a vibration. In the visible spectrum there are seven colors. Color theory may reduce them to three primary colors, but in the spectrum there are seven. Each color has an effect on the soul.

Red has its own vibrational resonance. It stands lower in the spectrum than violet, while violet is at the high end and red at the low. When the eye sees red, red stimulates a person, even when the person does not consciously know it. Modern studies in color theory have shown this. A red room affects people differently from a blue room, and the color can change their mood. These colors have resonance because they are electromagnetic radiation. They therefore leave a psychological effect, even when that effect is unnoticed.

The world shows the same mercy in green. Green brings ease to the heart. This is why people love looking at grass and trees. It has a , as the Arabs say. It is called . This is why I pray, “O Allah, make the Quran the spring of my heart,” and

I mean the thing that brings the heart back to life. Spring does this to the whole human being. People begin to feel well again. Some suffer from what is called SAD, “Seasonal Affective Disorder.” They become depressed in winter, then spring comes, and the heaviness of winter almost disappears from memory. They begin to feel wonderful.
The reason is green. The colors begin to change. Photosynthesis returns. Chlorophyll starts coming back to life. Flowers begin to bloom again.

I mean flowers themselves. What is a flower? Why do people love the scent of a flower? That is another of fragrance. Yet even before scent, there is the sight of a beautiful flower. Beauty itself arrests the eye.

When the eye rests on something beautiful, human beings tend to answer it in the same way. Most people share a common sense of beauty. The beautiful thing draws the soul toward it. That attraction exists because beauty is an attribute of God. What appears in the is a reflection of a Divine attribute of the . In truth, the attraction is to the Divine, though it may seem to be an attraction to the flower.

It is not the flower's passing beauty, the beauty that fades, that truly draws the heart. The real attraction is the beauty of the Divine showing itself through creation. Yet people often do not recognize this.

The eye itself holds many signs, and I rarely think about them as they deserve. The eyelashes and eyebrows both serve a purpose. When anything comes near the eye, the eyelids close by instinct and protect it. That alone is astonishing.
Even with the eye alone, reflection opens onto abundance. I see the of this in what is already known, while many blessings remain hidden, not yet understood.

I then consider light, the outer factor that makes the eye useful and allows sight itself. Sight can affect whether people feel happy or depressed. One reason often given for depression is a drop in serotonin, a key hormone in the feeling of happiness, and one factor in its release is light.

During the day, I take in light without even thinking about it. Melatonin is also tied to light. It is the hormone that brings sleepiness, which is why people who remain constantly under artificial light may have trouble sleeping. Yet the eye is what receives that light and helps govern these effects. The eye is, in this sense, directing the body. Tiredness, wakefulness, drowsiness, and sleep patterns are all affected through it, though I often fail to recognize this.
All of this concerns only the eye. I cannot enumerate all its blessings. That is one . That is only under discussion here. Within it are blessings beyond counting, without limit, and it is only one .

I understand the as the one who lives constantly with gratitude, whether the blessing is present or absent. This comes from complete certainty. It is a connected to , contentment with Allah. It is also a state of , because once love takes hold, nothing else remains in view.

That is the beauty of love. When I am in love, I may not even see faults, even when they are truly there. If I love Layla and someone says, “Layla did this,” or, “She did that,” anger rises at once: “What? Layla would never do that.” “No! I saw Layla do it.” “You are lying. You are a liar. Layla would not do that.” Why? Because the lover is in love with Layla. Whatever is said about her, he will not believe it. That is real love, and people scarcely know that kind of love anymore.

So if I am in love with Allah, I cannot see Him as doing anything that truly harms me or wrongs me. I say instead, “It is me. I did this to myself. Allah did not do that. Allah would not do that. I did it to myself.”

Or I understand that Allah is acting like a father who punishes his child. A father may punish a child while loving that child. Why does he punish him? Because he knows there is benefit for the child in the punishment. He is disciplining the child. He is bringing the child back. Through that punishment, he is reminding the child of something worse. If I see my child putting his hand into the fire, I slap his hand. Why am I doing that?

Because I want him to feel a small pain so that he does not suffer a much greater one. I know that the pain of a slap is nothing beside the pain of the flame. In the same way, when Allah gives us great tribulations, they are nothing beside the Hellfire. Nothing. If Allah purifies us to keep us from doing what He does not want us to do, then the realizes that this tribulation is the love of his Creator for him.
The Prophet once saw a mother nursing her child. The man of Allah, as they say, takes discernment from everything. He takes , discernment and a lesson. There is a lesson in everything.

His glance is discernment, and his speech is wisdom. There is a reason he speaks. The Prophet once saw a woman nursing her child, and he said to his , “Do you think that this woman would throw her child into the Fire?” And they said, . She would never do that. He said, “Allah has more mercy for His servants than this woman has for her child.”
Allah has more mercy for His servants than this woman has for her child. Allah said about His Prophet
"O offspring of those whom We carried with Nuh !! Verily, he was a grateful slave."

I see people grow weary after a single week of , and they say that such people will never listen. But this was 950 years of doing what Allah commanded him to do. That is . One report in mentions that never once went to relieve himself except that he returned saying, ; praise be to the One who removed this harm from me. He even had for something as ordinary as relieving himself, because that too is a blessing.
I recall that once went to visit . He asked , “Would you like anything?” said, “Bring me a glass of water.”
So water was brought to him. asked, “If this water were withheld from you, and you were dying of thirst, what would you give for it?”
He said, “I would give half my kingdom for it, if I could not have it.”
He said, “If you drank that water and then could not release it, what would you give in order to release it?”
He said, “The rest of my kingdom.”
said, “Then what is the worth of your kingdom, if it is not worth a cup of water, or the release of it as urine?”
In other words, what do I truly possess, if it does not equal a cup of water, or the release of it as urine?

I consider even the blessing of eating, and the fact that digestion follows without command. I do not have to tell hydrochloric acid to be released. I do not press any button. I eat, and if the food contains protein, the body breaks it into amino acids, then rebuilds it as muscle tissue. If it contains fat, the body breaks it into fatty acids, then reassembles what it needs. If it contains carbohydrates, the body breaks them down and carries their benefit to the brain, producing energy.

If there is more than is needed at once, insulin is released. It carries the surplus to the liver and stores it as glycogen, so that when energy runs low, the liver can release that glycogen and break it down to produce energy. I did not have to instruct the body to do any of this. Yet all of it is being done for us. ! Islam is gratitude to Allah. That is what Islam is.

At this moment, I am at about 98 degrees. Who is maintaining my body at 98.6 right now? I could have a fever. I could be shivering. If I were sick now — — even in a room with a moderate temperature, I could feel cold and shiver, though the room itself was not cold. If I had a fever, I could feel as if I were burning in that same moderate climate.

The people around me might feel perfectly well. Yet if fever had overtaken me, I would want to throw off my clothes from the heat. The matter deserves real reflection. Allah is keeping us near this 98.6 degrees. Even when it is a hundred degrees outside, the body releases fluid so it can hold that average temperature, or close to it.

If the air outside is a hundred degrees, why does the body not rise and boil up to a hundred degrees? What created that inner thermostat, the one that keeps the body in balance? If it is cold outside, why does the body not immediately drop and freeze? It can happen. If I remain long enough in freezing temperatures, I will freeze. But for a time, I do not. My temperature holds near 98.6. I can swim in cold water, and my temperature still maintains itself. All of this is from Allah .
As , I remain constantly aware of the abundance of these blessings from the . At the same time, I look at those who have less than I do in worldly affairs, and from that sight I draw gratitude.

There is a hadith in which Rasul Allah said about that a person should look at those below him in , because that keeps gratitude alive. There are always people who have less. However miserable my own state may seem, I can always find people in greater misery than I am facing now. Then I say, .

If I do not have much money, the measure still changes with time and place. In this country, people like me are rich. In Biblical times, placing a jar of honey on the table was a sign of great wealth. A jar of honey on the table truly marked wealth. Most people living in America would have been considered royalty in any earlier age. They would have been seen as living in palaces.

I think of what it means to have running water in this country. Even in the 1930s, about 70 percent of Americans still did not have it. Running water itself is a mercy. A hot shower comes by turning a knob, and people hardly think about it.

There are places in the world that , where women spend their whole day bringing water. For some of them, the trip takes about two hours to reach the water, about an hour to fill the containers, and two hours to return. Five hours every day, only to bring drinking water back to the village. That is their life. That is the whole shape of it. They have to load the donkeys with the .
What must they feel when they drink water? this . Their water is brown. It is brown. Most of them have kidney problems. Most of them have urinary problems because of the sediment in the water.
People have forgotten this. I could have been born in that village, drinking that brown water and living with those kidney problems. I rarely think about these things.
I think about the of the house I live in. I think about the of water, the of food on my table, the of clothes that cover my nakedness and keep me warm, and the of a bed.

I think about the of being healthy: , that I got up this morning and was not sick. Many people woke this morning and had to empty a bag filled with their urine, a bag they must change every day. Many woke unable to use the toilet, or bleeding blood. Many people with asthma woke unable to breathe, gasping for air. Many spent last night coughing and could not sleep because of it.
That is why even a simple is a way of showing gratitude to Allah .
I have to wonder about my life. I look at the blessings that has given me, and then I look at my complaints.

I say, “What did I do to deserve this?” I exist. That alone is enough as a crime. If I think seriously about it, that is enough: to imagine that I possess existence beside Allah. To imagine that I share existence with Allah. I am a criminal, because . There is nothing worthy of worship but Allah.

Yet here I am, walking around as a small contingent creature on an insignificant planet, in an insignificant galaxy. I depend on Allah for every breath, at every instant, and still I imagine that I am independent. I imagine that I am self-sufficient. I imagine that I am in control.

If I live in such heedlessness before Allah , I am a criminal. If I forget Allah for even one instant, I am a criminal, and I stand condemned. Whatever happens to me, I deserve it, because I have forgotten who I am and who Allah is.
O man! What has made you careless concerning your Lord, the Most Generous?

What has deluded me about my Master? What has deluded me about my Lord? Why am I in a state of , in total delusion? I imagine that I do not need Him at every instant of my life, even to take the next breath, even to receive the next heartbeat.

What is a heartbeat? It is an electrical impulse. Who activates it? It is Allah . I may think it is my brain, but it is not my brain. The brain is not doing that. They do not even know what causes it. All the nerves to the brain can be cut, and the heart still beats. What, then, makes the heart beat?
And yet here I am among these insignificant creatures, complaining about Allah , judging Him for His faults . That is a crime.

Or I sit on a high horse, as though beside Him, judging other people. Our look down on others because of knowledge Allah has blessed them with. Allah did not give that knowledge so it could become a reason to look down on anyone. He created us all as brothers, so that we would embrace one another.
There are two kinds of embrace:
the embrace of an equal the embrace of a superior
The embrace of an equal is simple. I embrace someone who stands with me as a brother. I put my arms around him, and he puts his arms around me.
The embrace of a superior toward an inferior is different. It is the embrace given to a child. The child cannot put his arms around me. I pick him up, embrace him, and hold him.
That is Islam. The , the temperament of Islam, is to take all those other sects and religions, and all those who are inferior in knowledge, and embrace them.

That is the embrace of Allah . He is so great that He allows even someone who denies Him to exist. That is greatness. That is . He feeds him, nurtures him, gives him rain, keeps his body healthy, and gives him a wife and children who love him. Allah does all of this even though that person denies His very existence. It only shows the greatness of God.

I know the story of . He never ate alone. He always found someone to share his food. One night, however, he found no one, so he went out searching until he came across a man and brought him home. The man was a .
Before eating, the man blessed his food in the names of his idols. When heard this, he said, “You can't eat any of my food. You're an idol worshiper, Get out of here!” The man left.
Then Allah revealed to that man: “I have been feeding him for 40 years and I've been patient with his idolatry for 40 years. You couldn't be patient with him for one meal?”
So went out, found the man, apologized to him, and invited him back to his table. The man asked him why, and he told him. Then the man became Muslim. That is Islam.

I can embrace them. matters here because in Arabic means an invitation. If I put a gun to someone's head and said, “You are coming to dinner tonight at my house,” that would not be an invitation. It would be force.

An invitation is real only when the invited person has room to refuse. The host who allows that possibility is a generous host. Allah has made a house, and He called it . He invited His creation to it, and He gave them the choice not to come. If people refuse that invitation, I have no reason to fear them.

Ignorant people fear difference. That fear is what marks a fundamentalist: someone afraid of the other, afraid of having his challenged, so afraid that he cannot allow the other to exist. He does not accept even the possibility of their presence. He wants them eliminated. That is a disease. Islam is the only religion that has allowed other religions and other ideologies to live beside it.
Praise
One of the great scholars of Islam said that the door through which he came to his Lord was , exalting the creation of Allah, . He said:
I never saw a scholar except that I honored him for the knowledge he carried. But then it reached a point where

I never saw a believer, or any Muslim man, whatever his condition, except that I honored him simply because he was a servant of Allah, trying to submit to Him. Then he said that he no longer saw anyone, even among the non-Muslims, without that same regard.

except that I exalted him, because in his very existence I saw the Divine will appearing before my eyes. Then he said that he never saw a rock, a tree, or anything at all except as a manifestation of the Divine will. God had placed that thing there. That was what he acknowledged. Then he said:

I understand this to mean that the one who exalts the , the sanctified things of God, is the one most loved by Allah. In this , what is more sanctified than the creation of Allah, ? These things Allah has created are His , His Divine manifestations. They call forth wonder and praise. They draw out from within the human being the praise that belongs to the .

When people see someone do something remarkable, the same movement appears in the heart. A beautiful singer sings a song, or a musician plays an instrument in a concert, and the audience claps, whistles, and gives an ovation. They praise the artist because something has happened inside them. They have witnessed something extraordinary, and it has touched the soul.

When a person who has mastered the piano stands and plays an extraordinary piece by Beethoven, people rise to their feet and keep clapping. Their response says, in effect, “What an extraordinary thing you have just done before our eyes. It was truly incredible.” That is what they feel moved to do, because what they have seen is so amazing.

I stand within an astonishing existence, a theater of extraordinary creation: stars in the heavens, whole galaxies of them, and telescopes that look toward the farthest edges of the universe, into its vast expanse. Flowers bloom before my eyes. Some move as the sun moves across the sky, following its course; the Arabs call them .

Animals do remarkable things. Elephants carry immense weight on their backs. Ants, even more astonishing in the delicacy of their creation, carry many times their own weight. These signs unfold in front of me.

In the womb, a child develops from a fetus, with cells dividing rapidly through mitosis. This is happening everywhere, all the time. Yet I do not feel compelled to rise in praise before Allah? I do not stand before Allah and say, “Allah. Allahu Akbar. Allahu Akbar. Allahu Akbar”?

I can stand in ovation before some poor soul who has perfected a small trick on a musical instrument, who can pipe out a tune, and feel moved to leap up, clap, and say, “Bravo, bravo.” Yet I cannot rise to praise the Master of the worlds, the and , and say, “Allahu Akbar”? What has happened to me?
What has deluded me? What has drawn me away from the praise of my Master?

Our Prophet constantly went into out of gratitude. When he saw an eclipse, he rose and gave God an ovation. He prayed. He stood and prayed, then went into , bearing witness that he had seen a reminder. Yet such reminders are present in every instant.

May Allah strengthen my heart to witness, experience, and marvel at the blessings of his and his . May he help me taste the joy of true and sincere praise, and of unconditional gratitude, not only for everything he has given me, but also for what he has withheld. Not only for the joy in my life, but also for the grief and sorrow that humble me, pull me off my high horse, and bring me back down to the earth.
I have now set out the linguistic meanings of the basic terms, so I begin with , the first verse of .

I find that the Arabs often shortened statements that were used again and again. When they wanted to refer to , they referred to it by . When they wanted to refer to , they called it the . In the same way, they used for , and so on.
Being vs Attributes

From a grammatical point of view, contains one noun and two adjectives. The word Allah is a noun. It names an entity, a being. Then two attributes of are mentioned, and they describe the nature of Allah: and .

I now turn to the distinction between Allah's name and his attributes. In grammatical terms, this is the distinction between a noun and adjectives. Attributes are among the tools language gives for understanding something. Through noun and adjectives together, or through name and attributes together, I understand an entity.

I gain a fuller understanding of any entity by understanding its attributes. In Arabic, this relation is called and : being and its attributes. For example, I have a soul and a body, and together they constitute my , my being.

The soul has spiritual attributes: kindness, courage, intelligence, generosity, or, by contrast, weakness, cowardice, and dullness. The body has physical attributes: fatness or thinness, blackness, brownness, whiteness, height, or shortness. Once I understand the spiritual and physical attributes that describe the soul and the body, I recognize the nature of their being. The union of being and attributes gives identity its full description and allows the intellect to understand what that being is.

Yet attributes cannot exist without being. The gives existence to the . Attributes come only after the being itself exists. If there is no , there can be no and no . For this reason, the name Allah is greater than and , because it comes first.
I can now break down the statement of the . The term Allah points to His , His being. He is a deity named Allah. Allah is the title of His essence.

No doubt, I am Allah; and there is none worthy of worship and obedience except me. This noun Allah has adjectives: His ninety-nine , His attributes, which describe the nature of Allah and His various manifestations in His dealings with creation. I now have,

I understand these names as attributes that describe the nature of Allah. I have used the example of a prism and light before: Allah may be understood as one pure light, . When the pure light of the name Allah enters the physical realm, his divine attributes refract within creation.

From that refraction, the many manifestations of Allah's essence become known through his dealings with creation. In one instance, Allah is (the generous). In another, he is (the compeller). In another, he is (the subduer). In another, he is (the powerful). In another, he is (the one who humiliates and humbles). In another, he is (the one who bestows honor).

His essence appears through all these attributes within creation. The world therefore becomes a theater for the divine manifestations of Allah's attributes, and through them I come to know Allah: not directly through his essence, but through the refraction of his attributes in his creation.
Transcendence vs immanence
This is why it is said:

I do not reflect upon Allah directly, but reflect instead upon the creations of Allah. Creation, and the natural world within it, is where his attributes become visible to me. Yet Allah is infinite, and his attributes are infinite. For that reason, when I try to understand Allah, I become bewildered by his attributes. In one sense, I cannot know what God is any more than I can know what God is not. Speech about Allah is speech about the infinite creator of the heavens and the earth. Infinite means without limit: .

In Arabic, the word for “definition” is also the word used for limitation, or boundary: . A definition gives a concept its finiteness. It limits it, marks its edges, and sets it in perspective. Therefore, when I speak about God, I cannot define God. To define God would be to give him a , a boundary, and a limit. That is impossible. This is why the scholars say that all of can be reduced to two statements:
He is unlike anything.
His essence is not like any other essence, and his attributes are not metaphorical in any way. He is:
He has no need of anyone, and everyone is in need of him. This statement negates need for Allah: . It also negates independence for me.

I now come to another central problem in religion: transcendence and immanence. Transcendence means speaking about God without taking anything in the world as a guide to Him. Nothing in the world can be pointed to and called God.

Allah is above and beyond whatever they ascribe to Him. When I speak about transcendence, I mean that Allah is above and beyond everything I know: . In Arabic this is called . The word means transcendence. It comes from , which means to purify, to remove filth, and to rise beyond something.

Allah is transcendent. Yet pure transcendence brings serious problems. It turns Him into the God of the scientist. Einstein, for example, believed in a god, but not in a personal god. He believed in a transcendent god. The god he believed in was the God of the deist: a god with nothing to do with his creation. That is a major problem.

The other problem appears in what is called immanence: the idea that God is present within the world. In the Hindu tradition, for example, the Brahman class does not truly believe in the idols. The idols function as a kind of device for ordinary people, who are thought still to need something visible before they can rise to a higher understanding.

Within that tradition, the lower classes of the caste system are called the VERNA. A person in a lesser varna is not thought able to understand the BRAHMA. The Brahman has passed through many lifetimes and has reached the capacity to perceive. Only he can perceive, and only he can understand the Godhead, which they call the Brahma.

So the Brahman understands a god without attributes, which they call the NIRGOONA. Yet they also hold that lower-class people need to see something before they can understand it. For that reason, they gave them idols, while knowing that these idols were not truly gods. The idols help the common people understand.

This is the problem of immanence in religion: it creates likeness. Christianity deals with this problem through Jesus, because Jesus becomes the incarnation of God. God enters into flesh. In our tradition, this is called , when God enters the flesh. Some deviant Sufis also claimed this state. The group called claimed it for Maulana Ali. It also happened for .
I ask how I understand this in my religion. What is the relationship between transcendence and immanence, between and ?

A servant must have access to his master. If God is understood as only transcendent, He becomes cold, distant, uncaring, and unloving. But if the attributes of creation are given to God, another problem appears. This is what gives birth to anthropomorphism: the idea that God is petulant, that He has emotions, anger, and pleasure in the way created beings do.
This problem also appears in some Muslim understandings. Some Muslims hear words used in hadith or in the Quran and take them in a human way.
They think that those who faced the anger of Allah faced an anger like ours. They imagine that Allah becomes angry in an emotional sense, and that:
Allah is above and beyond anything they ascribe to him.
At the same time, I do believe that has a meaning. I believe that has a meaning. I believe that the words Allah used in the Quran have meaning:

They were pleased with Allah, and Allah was pleased with them. But a person's pleasure with Allah is not the same as Allah's pleasure with that person. The two words do not carry the same meaning in the two contexts. Each word means something specific according to the thing it is predicated of.
So when I speak about the attributes of Allah, , I must be extremely careful. In one sense, I can only say about Allah what Allah has said about himself.

I then meet another difficulty: the difficulty of interpretation. Allah tells me about Himself and discloses Himself to me, but He does so through language. Language reaches me through the human mind, and the human mind can understand what it hears in many different ways.

For this reason, the Prophet is the purest filter. He is still a filter, because he is human. But he is the purest human filter. This is part of what sets the prophets apart from other human beings: Allah chose them to be the filters through which revelation reaches creation.
So the soundest understanding of Allah is the understanding the Prophet gave us. This is why he said:

I am not able to praise You as You deserve. You are as You praised Yourself. In other words, I cannot truly praise You, because praise depends on knowledge of the one being praised. Without knowing the qualities of someone or something, real praise is not possible.

This is why, in Allah's self-disclosure to us, He describes the reasons He is worthy of praise. He is . He has told us about His praiseworthy attributes. Through those attributes, I come to know Allah.

These attributes are known through human experience. Here the problem of immanence appears. There must be some relation between what I understand about Allah and what I understand about myself, or what I see in the world. Without that relation, knowing Allah would not be possible.

So when I speak about the attributes of Allah, I am still working with things known in the world. When I say that Allah is , the word becomes difficult because it is a technical term. It is not found in the Quran, and it is not itself an attribute of Allah. It was used as a technical expression.

is a attribute because it negates ; it negates occurrence. It denies that Allah came into existence. No. The meaning of is that Allah is as He always was, and that He will always remain the same, without change and without any factor of time.

Success stands between them, in the balance of knowledge and action. That balance is the true manifestation of : that I obey through knowledge, strive to understand the wisdom in my master's commands, and then act upon them in practice. In this way, I demonstrate my for my master.

cues.text: The Preposition BA

I now turn to the letter , a preposition that means “with” or “in.” In the phrase , the meaning is: I begin in the name of Allah. The verb “I begin” is not spoken, but it is understood. In grammar this is called .

The reason is that the of is attached to an omitted verb. This point matters because a verb, or an action, is the basis of all existence. If the basis of existence were treated as a noun, the discussion would remain at the level of a state. For example, the human state of being would mean simply that I am here, that I exist here, with no action involved in that being.

A verb changes the matter because it brings time into it. An action belongs to past, present, or future. Nouns do not. A tree is a tree. But when the tree begins to blow in the wind, time enters the picture. Did it blow in the past? Is it blowing now? Will it blow when the wind comes?

The tree's swaying is an action of the tree's essence. Without that action, the tree is simply in a state of being. This opens a deeper question about existence itself: is the root of existence movement and action, or is it being?

I hold that the same point applies to Allah's relationship with the world. Allah has action, but his action is created. His actual essence is passive. When I speak about Allah , there is no action in his essence.

Allah is essence and attribute, and both essence and attribute are states of being. Action, however, is a substantive: it enters time and takes place within it. For this reason, theology understands that Allah is beyond time and space. His action, then, appears as creation and within creation. He brings things into existence through his , but that is .

When he decides an affair, he says to it "be" and it "is". Allah brings creation into existence through a command, which is a . The preposition is therefore connected to the omitted verb of Allah's act of creation.

When I recite the , I am saying . I begin with the recognition of the lofty signs within Allah's creation. These signs bear witness to His intense and constant love, compassion, care, and mercy. This is the context of Allah's primordial act, . In other words, this is the meaning of that statement in the transcendent realm. Its meaning in the immanent, personal realm is another matter.
Omitted Verb
That meaning becomes clearer when I break the statement into its grammatical parts. I recite the at the beginning of every action. Grammatically, the statement has these components:
It begins with the letter , which is a preposition.

Then comes the word , a genitive masculine noun. On its own, this noun is written as “,” meaning “the name.” Because it is joined to the preposition, the is dropped, and the fuses with the to become , making it an indefinite noun.
Then comes the proper noun Allah.
Finally, the statement ends with two adjectives of mercy: and .

So the statement contains a preposition, an indefinite noun, a proper noun, and two adjectives. From a grammatical point of view, something is still missing: a verb. A statement is grammatically incomplete without one.

Allah left the phrase as an incomplete sentence. He omitted the verb. The reason is that I complete the sentence in meaning by supplying the verb through my own action. This is why I recite the at the beginning of every action and every task: my action provides the missing verb and completes the structure of the statement. SubhanAllah.

If I am about to read the Quran and I say , the act of reading completes the . What I am saying is: “With the name of Allah, who is intensely and consistently loving and merciful, I begin reading this book.” Whatever the action may be, it is strengthened by the .

What is even more remarkable appears when I look at the phrase linguistically, in light of what has already been learned. I am really saying that my ability to read, and the Quran I intend to read, are both lofty signs pointing to Allah's immense love and mercy: His and His . The moment I recite this phrase, Allah's love and mercy stand at the center of my attention. My act, whatever it is, becomes a lofty sign and symbol. It becomes a witness and bears testimony to Allah's . It changes my view of the action before I have even begun it. SubhanAllah.

When I say before I begin driving, the whole act of driving becomes a reminder of Allah's love and mercy. My ability to drive points back to Him. So do the resources that allow me to own a car, the mental capacity to read the signs, the judgment to assess traffic, the intuition to know when to stop and how fast to go, the facilities inside the car, and the scenery outside it. Every part of the experience becomes a lofty reminder that points me directly to Allah's intense and constant love, care, concern, and mercy for me. SubhanAllah. This is the power of .

SubhanAllah. It is astonishing. Allah's first act was based on this : He gave me the ability to act, and every act I perform becomes a witness to His love and mercy. All of that is gathered inside the phrase . I begin this task, this action, as a lofty heavenly sign that reminds me of Allah's intense and constant love, care, concern, and mercy.
Allah and his name

The purpose of reciting before I begin an action is clear from my side: it reminds me of Allah's love and mercy, and it naturally makes me love Him in return. That love appears as worship and obedience, as my . From Allah's side, it fills my action with . As Allah said:

When you obey me, it pleases me. When I am pleased, I bless you with , and there is no limit to my . What is ? It is abundance. What, then, does abundance have to do with ? What does it have to do with the of Allah?
Allah says in .
Blessed be the Name of your Lord, the Owner of Majesty and Honor.

I begin with the name of Allah. The name of the master is glorious and generous; his name is full of . Yet in this verse Allah does not specify which name is full of . He says only that the name of the master is full of .
This Surah itself began with . The first attribute of Allah mentioned in the is again . Allah is therefore showing that the attribute is full of .
I also know that Allah himself is full of , because he says so in the Quran.
So blessed is Allah , the best of creators
Allah, the best of creators, is full of .

I see, then, that the of Allah is full of , and that the name Allah itself is full of . The first two words of the are therefore heavy with : and . When I recite these two powerful words before beginning an act, that act is filled with . In other words, by reciting , I am not only reminding myself of Allah's intense and constant love and mercy through the act itself; I am also asking Him to fill that act with .
Abundance
What, then, is ?
No word in English can fully carry the meaning of . I therefore have to understand this word through several related ideas.
Abundance
In classical Arabic, the word is defined as

I understand it as growth and abundance. The first sense is , which means growth: something that rises, increases in size, makes steady progress, produces ever greater results, and goes further than expected. This is .

When the seed of a single fruit is placed in the ground, ordinary expectation would look for one fruit in return. Instead, that one seed can become a tree that bears an enormous number of fruits, and each fruit may carry hundreds or thousands of seeds. That is . One seed was planted, and in the end thousands of seeds appeared. This is growth beyond expectation. This is what I call .

The comparison between a seed and a tree almost collapses. A seed is tiny; a tree is vast. A seed is delicate; a tree is firm. A seed seems to have little value; a tree bears fruit upon fruit, season after season, year after year. What comes from the tree, when set beside the seed, is beyond comparison. Yet the whole tree came from that one seed. SubhanAllah. That is : unprecedented growth and unbounded increase.
Never Ending
The Arabs say for rain that keeps falling and keeps falling. Continuity, then, is another quality carried by the word . It means something extensively abundant.
Stability
The word is also used in Arabic for stability. An Arab would say . When a camel settles on the ground and does not move or budge, that too is .

This is a beautiful meaning, because when something grows too much, growth often makes it less steady. A simple example is the way children build with Lego. They stack one block on another until a huge tower rises. As the tower grows taller, it does not become more stable. It becomes less stable. The higher it goes, the more likely it is to fall and break, until no tower remains.

So when something increases very quickly, and increases too much, it usually becomes less stable. But when something has in it, it increases in quantity and keeps increasing beyond expectation, while remaining as stable as a camel sunk into the sand. SubhanAllah. This increase is not something that will simply vanish. It is not unstable growth.

Unstable growth appears everywhere in the world. An economy rises very fast, then crashes very fast. Governments sometimes take power quickly, then disappear just as quickly. The fashion industry works the same way: trends pick up fast, then vanish, and something else takes their place. But Allah says is an increase that remains stable. It does not go away.
Abundance through Allah's name

When I speak the name of Allah, , I speak a name filled with . The name Allah itself is filled with . His blessed name has been mentioned from the day creation came into being, and with every passing moment its mention only increases and grows. It will continue to grow until the end of time.

Worshipers come and go, but the One who is worshiped remains forever. Those who glorify the names of Allah come and go. Many came before us, and many will come after us. One day I will be gone, and so will all of us, but the glory of Allah will always remain. This is the of Allah's name.

So, when I recite before every action I do, that action itself becomes a reminder. It becomes a heavenly, lofty sign pointing to the loving care and mercy of and in my life. That brings into the results of my action. There is a hadith of Rasul Allah in which he said:
I understand from that every single act is barren without the remembrance of Allah. It has no in it and no true abundance.

Abundance frees a person from need and fear. When money is abundant, for example, it removes and in that one part of life. It loosens the chains of anxiety and sadness, because that concern no longer dominates the heart.

The matter is far greater when there is an unending supply of Allah's and in life. When I have abundant , that close connection with Allah, no situation can truly overcome me, however painful it may be. It cannot make the heart collapse into anxiety or despair, because whatever the outward result may be, the act itself becomes an experience of nearness, joy, and Allah's love. SubhanAllah.

This is what Rasul Allah meant when he said that everything is sterile and infertile without . Without Allah's love and nearness to Allah, no amount of material plenty can satisfy the soul in this world.

I see the clearest proof of this hadith in the world around me. There are millionaires and billionaires who live in deep anxiety and constant depression. At the same time, I see true Muslims and believers who remain content and happy even in the hardest circumstances. The reason is their connection to Allah. That connection places in the little they possess until they are pleased, content, and satisfied with it, so much so that they do not even crave more. SubhanAllah. This is the of .
I ask Allah to fill my heart with Allah's love, and to make every action I do from this day onward an experience of Allah's love and mercy.

cues.text: This book is a series of spoken sessions, delivered aloud to an audience and afterward set down as prose. It takes the opening chapter of the Quran, Surah Al-Fateha, and reads it slowly, almost phrase by phrase, drawing out of each word far more than a first hearing would suggest is there.

The series belongs to a larger conversation about knowing one's master. It begins where the speaker says understanding must begin: not with theology but with friendship, and from friendship with love, because the name Allah reaches back to a root the sessions approach through the Quranic idea of love. From there the talks move outward — the linguistic meaning of Allah, of Rabb, of REHMA, and the striking image of the womb as the source of mercy. They ask what worship truly is, what it means that Allah is the Lord of all the worlds, and how being differs from attribute. They turn to the Day of Judgment, to the motives that move a person toward piety, and at last to the two petitions the surah teaches us to make: guidance to the straight path, and the steadfastness to remain upon it.
The speaker is the author of these sessions; he gave them, and they carry his voice throughout. What the reader receives is a patient, close reading meant to make a familiar prayer new again.
I now turn to the Surah. The first of is
ILAH

I begin with the word . The word Allah comes from the root word , a term I generally use to mean God. In reality, however, is a very general term, comparable to words such as "book" or "car." There are many kinds of books and cars; neither term is specific. In the same way, there can be many kinds of . English has two kinds of articles: the indefinite article "a," as in "a book" or "a car," and the definite article "the," as in "the book" or "the car."
A vs THE

The distinction between "a book" and "the book" is important. "A book" is generic and could refer to any book. But when I say "the book," I am no longer referring to just any book; I have a particular book in mind. The same principle applies to the word .
ILAH vs AL-ILAH

The word is a generic, indefinite term that may apply to many things. There can be many kinds of , just as there can be many kinds of books. But when the Arabic definite article , meaning "the," is attached to it, the combination + produces the word . In other words, is the specific, definite form of the generic word . At its root, Allah is + . By the rules of Arabic grammar, the of is dropped, and the merges with the and the to become Allah. To understand the linguistic meaning of the word Allah, then, the first step is to understand the meaning of .
Composite Words

The word is a compound word that carries a range of meanings. A composite word may be compared to a jigsaw puzzle: each piece carries a distinct meaning, and all the pieces together form the complete picture. If carries four meanings — A, B, C, and D — then a full understanding of the word comes from all four taken together. Its meaning is not A alone, nor B alone, nor C or D in isolation. It is A + B + C + D. This is what I mean by a composite word, and the concept is worth keeping firmly in mind because many of the words examined in these pages are composite words of this kind.
Meanings Of Word ILAH
The word carries several distinct meanings, each of which contributes to the whole.
YALAA
The primary root is , drawn from . At its core, the verb means to worship. The first meaning of , therefore, is: the one who is the object of all worship and obedience.

Worship itself is an extreme form of gratitude — the highest degree of thankfulness, in which the one who has given becomes so precious and indispensable that the heart is brought to its knees. It is a state of complete surrender when a person's will yields entirely to the will of the beloved. When that happens, the beloved becomes one's . This is the first meaning of .

The principle extends into ordinary life. A person who is so consumed by a career that it is placed above every other person and every competing claim has made that career an . Whatever commands and rules the heart, whatever a person effectively bows before — whether video games, sport, television, children, or wealth — fits this definition. Such things become, in a meaningful sense, an . Likewise, when love for another person becomes so total that it governs every thought, action, and decision, that beloved has become an . For is precisely this: the one worshipped, the one obeyed and submitted to without question.
ALAHA

The word is also used for a child desperate for its mother's milk, crying out for it with everything it has — that, too, is . There is a particular hunger in a baby's face at such a moment, and a particular intensity in the way it reaches for its mother. That is : the one to whom a person turns desperately and inevitably, with passion and need, in moments of happiness and grief alike, without restraint or control. That, too, is an .

Some people are enslaved to sugar; others to cigarettes, drugs, parties, or films. Whatever a person turns to desperately and uncontrollably the moment happiness or depression strikes, whatever becomes the source of relief and comfort, is by this definition their . Peace is sought in its arms. Obedience to it no longer feels like a choice but a compulsion. When the craving commands a person to smoke, the person obeys. When the desire for ice cream becomes irresistible, the person obeys. Watching one more episode or spending hours every day playing video games may cease to be merely casual habits and become acts of total loyalty and devotion, driven by the conviction that happiness and satisfaction are impossible without them. The person turns to these things with the same desperation with which a baby, burning with thirst, turns to its mother.

This applies to every one of us. We all have such in our lives. That does not make us horrible people; it makes us human. By learning these meanings, we begin to recognize these masters for what they are. That recognition is the first step toward change.
WALAHA

The next word is . It describes someone with whom one is passionately in love — someone one cannot stop thinking about, someone who occupies the mind completely. The derivative is used when a person is driven to madness by the loss of a beloved. A mother who loses her child is called : a mother enduring the excruciating pain and grief of her child's loss. She is called . It is this kind of passionate, consuming love. In Urdu, the expression is — mad love, crazy love — and that, too, comes from . When someone in one's life has that kind of hold on the heart — when one thinks of that person constantly, when separation drives one to the edge of reason, when one cannot stop calling or texting, when one repeatedly returns to old photographs and messages, missing that person with every part of oneself — that is the state of , and by definition that person is one's .
ALIHA

The next meaning, , applies literally — not linguistically — to something on which a person leans, something that bears their full weight. When exhaustion sets in and one leans against something, that supporting thing is literally called . Thus, if the weight of life rests on finances, property, houses, cars, a job, social standing, friends, neighbors, or children — anything on which one psychologically leans — then each of those things is an . Whatever holds all one's eggs in a single basket, so to speak, becomes one's .
WALIHA

Another derivative of comes from , which means to become astounded, astonished, or mesmerized. People make role models of actors, musicians, and hip-hop artists. This is especially true of young people who want to be like them, live like them, think like them, dress like them, talk like them, and walk like them. When someone shaves his head to look like Amir Khan in the film Gajni, he has made Amir Khan his . By definition, is the one by whom a person is completely and utterly captivated — the one to imitate, the one to become. It may be a person, an object, a profession, or anything else. Whatever mesmerizes and grips a person so completely that it takes control of their decisions becomes their .
These, then, are the various meanings gathered into the word . Returning to the question: who or what is an ?

The one worshipped and obeyed is one's . The one to whom complete devotion and loyalty are given is one's . The one to whom a person turns in utter desperation, seeking comfort, is one's . The one a person loves passionately, the one who becomes an obsession, is one's . The one on whom a person leans for support — physically, mentally, emotionally, or psychologically — is one's .

This, then, is what the word means. And because is a composite word, it carries the sum of all these meanings at once. The one a person passionately loves is also the one to whom that person is completely devoted; the one on whom they lean; the one to whom they turn desperately for comfort and support. Separation or distance from that person drives them to the edge of sanity. They submit to and obey everything that person says — they worship that person, in the fullest sense described here. All these meanings converge to form a single, complete picture. That is how a composite word works.
Given these meanings of , it becomes clear that every person carries numerous in their life, embodying these definitions in countless forms:

Some take the form of people — family, friends, children, parents, actors, musicians. Some take the form of objects — houses, cars, one's own body, jewelry, food, video games, movies. Some take the form of pursuits and compulsions — jobs, careers, recreation, drugs, sex.
Every person carries hundreds, if not thousands, of entities in their life that meet the definition of .
idols

What follows is where the discussion becomes uncomfortable. Every person and thing in our lives that meets the definition of gives physical form to one of the meanings of that word. By definition, is the one to whom we are loyal and devoted; is the one to whom we turn for comfort. So if smoking, movies, or video games are what someone turns to for comfort, those activities become a physical manifestation of that definition of . The definition is conceptual; its manifestation is physical. A person physically does something to please that .

Consider another definition: is the one who astounds and astonishes. If Shahrukh Khan, Sylvester Stallone, Adele, Beyonce, or Lady Gaga are the ones who astound, astonish, and impress a person to the point that they want to be like them, then the definition of has been given a form. That definition has been personified in Shahrukh Khan, Stallone, or whoever else it may be.
as Idols

An idol, by dictionary definition, is an image or representation of a god used as an object of worship — the personification or objectification of someone or something. Idols are human creations. And who personifies and objectifies the definitions of ? We do. We decide to turn to smoking, movies, drugs, and alcohol for comfort. We decide to give our complete loyalty and devotion to our jobs, careers, Facebook, and Instagram. We choose to fall passionately in love with wealth, power, and fame. No one makes those choices for us. We make them ourselves. In this sense, we become the creators of our own , just as idols are human-made creations. The similarity is exact.

A common assumption is that being Muslim places a person entirely outside the world of idol worship. The frightening reality, according to this understanding, is otherwise. We are surrounded by thousands of — self-created idols — and we worship them daily. Every person, object, concept, and idea that we personify or objectify becomes, through that act, an idol fashioned by our own hands. In that sense, we are all idol-worshippers. It is a painful reality, but it is true. The concept of is not so alien after all. This is precisely why Rasul Allah said:
Shirk is more hidden in my nation than the movement of a black ant in a dark night on a black stone.
That is how unaware we may be of our own idol worship.

At the center of all my idols stands one figure: myself. And what drove me to fashion these ? My desires. Every idol I have ever built is a product of my passions and caprice; each exists because I wanted it to exist. Allah says:
Have you seen the one who takes his own desire as his god?

Allah is asking the messenger whether he sees this person — the one who has taken his car, house, job, wealth, fame, and the pleasures and sensations of his body as his ; the one who has taken smoking, drugs, alcohol, sex, movies, and video games as his ; the one who has taken Shahrukh Khan, Salman Khan, Amir Khan, Adele, and Stallone as his . Allah asks Rasul Allah ,
Do you really want to be responsible for this person on the day of judgment?

Worship of the self is the worst form of there is. When gratitude curdles into self-gratification, it becomes the worst kind of . Idolatry has nothing over self-idolatry. We are therefore the ones who continually commit by taking our desires and making them our . Human beings exist in a constant state of self-worship, and it is precisely this condition that prevents us from truly worshipping Allah.

This is the default condition of mankind. Islam addresses it at the root: through the negation and destruction of these self-created idols, the understanding of Allah emerges. Allah is — He is everything other than what is taken as . When every idol born of the desires of the self is broken and destroyed, when the Kaaba of the heart stands empty of them, what is found there is Allah.

The first act of Rasul Allah after the conquest of Mecca was to cleanse the Kaaba of all its idols. Three hundred and sixty-five idols stood in it, around it, and upon it. He destroyed every one without exception. That same exercise must be undertaken in every life. Just as Rasul Allah conquered Mecca, the must be conquered. Just as he cleared the Kaaba of its idols one by one, the Kaaba of the heart must gradually be cleared of these idols — one by one. And the greatest and most powerful idol standing in the Kaaba of the heart is the itself: the passions.

This is why the creedal formula strikes at the very root of the problem: . There is no except Allah. No person, thing, concept, principle, or ideology is worthy of being given form — except the one who is free of all form, and that is Allah. Through the negation of self-made idols and the elimination of self-created , the emerges. When the definite article joins , what results is the ultimate , Allah.
The creedal formula is the act of negating the multiplicity of self-created in order to affirm the one true , Allah. It is the practice of making into .

It is the practice of directing every definition of the word toward the one ultimate being — of making Him + , of making Him Allah. It is the work of isolating each definition of and making it specific to Allah alone.
Allah is now the only one I worship and obey. If any other conflicts with His commands, I disobey that in order to obey the + , which is Allah.

This does not mean that life cannot be enjoyed. The difference is that Allah now stands at the front and center of my worship and obedience. So long as nothing conflicts with that worship and obedience, I can enjoy life to the fullest.
now means : Allah is the only one to whom I am completely devoted and loyal, above everyone else in my life — even my parents, even my children. I serve only Allah and no one else.

Yet I am glad to serve my parents because Allah has commanded it. I am glad to spend time with my friends, to enjoy life, and to do whatever I wish, so long as my ultimate loyalty and devotion remain with Allah. Whenever anything or anyone challenges that loyalty, I choose Allah over them. That is how I make Him + .
now means : Allah is the only one to whom I turn in utter desperation for every need and every comfort.

This does not mean that I cannot seek help from family and friends. Nor does it mean that, when I am hungry and without work, I sit idle because Allah is the appointed provider. Not at all. I turn to whomever I need, for whatever I need. The difference is that I know these people are simply means — — through which Allah provides. My ultimate petition, therefore, is always addressed to Him: Ya Allah! I need this. I turn to you for the fulfillment of my needs. Provide me with the means and resources that will fulfill them in a way that pleases you. For it is you, and only you, who are the source of my provision — no one else.
now means : Allah is the one I love passionately, the one in whom I am completely absorbed. From the moment I wake until the moment I return to sleep, He is the one I think about.

This does not mean that I spend the entire day on the prayer rug or every hour in . I may do whatever I wish in life. But everything becomes a sign pointing toward Allah, a reminder of Him. That is what love does: the flower, the rainbow, the sunset, the frog in the pond — all recall the beloved. Love is an obsession. It is a constant connection with the beloved.

The story of Hazrat illuminates this. In a hadith of Rasul Allah , Allah spoke to His angels about the patience and gratitude of Hazrat AS. then addressed Allah directly, arguing that the only reason was grateful was because of the abundance he had been given — his wealth and his children. Strip those away, he said, and the gratitude would disappear. So Allah began to take them away. First the wealth went. Then, before his eyes, the house collapsed and killed all his sons. The word that rose instinctively to 's lips at that sight was AlHamdulillah. And if that were not enough, a terrible disease then descended upon him: his body became infected with worms that consumed his flesh. Allah put Hazrat through these extreme trials to test his faith and love, and he bore them with extraordinary grace. When the trial was complete, Allah directed him to bathe in a spring prepared for him. He bathed, and the disease was completely cured. Years later, someone asked him: How is your health now, ? He sighed and replied that the days of his illness had been more beloved to him than these days of health. The man was astonished and asked how that could be. replied that during his illness, Allah had asked him each day: How are you today, ? Now that he was cured, Allah no longer asked, and he missed the love and care that had been showered upon him during those days of trial. This is . This is — extreme, passionate love, in which the absence of the beloved drives a person to the very edge of self.
now means : Allah is the only one on whom I ultimately lean for support — emotionally, psychologically, financially, physically, in every form.

This does not mean that I will not see a doctor when I am ill, ask my employer for a raise when I deserve one, or turn to family and friends for help when I need it. I will continue to do all of that. But my ultimate support comes from Allah. He is the one who cures my illness, not the doctor. He is the one who ordains the raise, not my employer. He is the one who fulfills my need, not my friends and family.

The liberation this brings is immense. So many of my complaints about people and life would simply disappear. There is no longer any need to blame someone for a disappointment, because that person was never meant to be the one on whom I ultimately depended in the first place. Disappointment requires expectation. When all my ultimate expectations are from Allah, no one in this world can truly disappoint me. If I receive what I wanted, Allah was the one who gave it. If I do not receive it, it was not meant for me — and who can say that receiving it would not, in the long run, have proved harmful?
now means : Allah is the only one who ultimately astounds and impresses me.

This does not mean that I should appreciate no one, praise no one, or find no one impressive. It means that I see Allah behind every cause for praise. If my child does well in school — MashaAllah! Praise to Allah, who made my child capable. If I am mesmerized by the sunrise or sunset — SubhanAllah! Praise to Allah for creating this beauty, and for granting me the eyes, the time, and the willingness to appreciate it. I take the praise inspired by the beauty of the sunset and attribute it to its Creator.

Through this practice, the true concept of comes into view. is not the idea that Allah is the supreme deity within a hierarchy of deities. It is the recognition that there is no other deity at all. — the complete elimination of every other deity. — except the one and only, Allah. It is the transference of from its generic form to the one specific being who has no form. This is the challenge and the goal of .

The vehicle that carries a person along this path is Salaat. Within its very nature, Salaat contains the act of breaking idols. The moment the time for prayer arrives, whatever one is doing must stop, whoever one is attending to must be left, and the face must turn toward Allah. Salaat is enacted.

That is the journey of . It is a difficult journey, and every journey requires provisions to sustain the traveler. The provision for this journey is knowledge of Allah. The greater that knowledge, the greater one's amazement at His glory. The greater the amazement, the more passionate the love. The more passionate the love, the deeper the absorption. The deeper the absorption, the more complete the worship and submission to His commands. The more complete the worship, the more fully one turns to Him for refuge. The more one finds shelter under His protection, the more one leans on Him for support — for love engenders love. The more one comes to understand how deeply He loves, the more one loves in return. And the more that love grows, the more intensely His blessings and mercy are experienced.
And when your master proclaimed: "If you are grateful, I will give you more, but if you are ungrateful, indeed! My Punishment is indeed severe."
Salaat is the act of breaking idols. It begins with Wudu — the purification of the very parts of the body used in the service of those idols.

Noun vs Verbs
The grammar of this term sharpens the meaning. Language has nouns and verbs. Verbs carry tense; nouns do not. There is no past-tense noun, present-tense noun, or future-tense noun.

When I say, “I praise Allah,” I have used a verb, and that verb is in the present tense. But when Allah says that praise belongs to Allah, the word “praise” is a noun, not a verb. Allah could have used a verb. He could have said , “I praise Allah.” He could have said , “We praise Allah.” But Allah did not use a verb. He used a noun.

The difference matters because every verb carries a tense. If I use the present tense and say, “I praise Allah,” I am speaking only about the present. I have not said anything about the past or the future. If I use the past tense, I have not guaranteed anything about the present or the future. A verb confines an action within time. It makes the action temporary.
Allah used a noun, and a noun, by its nature, is not bound to a tense. It gives the meaning permanence. Therefore:

I understand Allah's true praise and unconditional gratitude as permanent. I may be praising Allah now, but the praise of Allah has always existed, and it will always remain. The sentence cannot simply say, “Failed the test!” because the question immediately rises: who failed the test? Nor can it simply say, “Disappeared!” because something must have disappeared. Only when the sentence says, “My book disappeared,” does the action have its subject.

A noun is different. A noun does not need a doer. It does not need a subject to make it stand. It is independent in itself. An apple is an apple; it can be named without attaching it to someone's action.

Even after this world and this universe fade into non-existence, His praise and gratitude will remain. It does not require a doer or an object. SubhanAllah. Responding in afflictions
I will give another example. There is a HADEES in which Rasul Allah tells us that when I visit a sick person, I should ask him to pray for me and for my forgiveness.

At first, that sounds reversed. I would expect myself to be the one praying for the sick person, asking Allah to grant him health. He appears to be the one in need of my prayers. Yet the HADEES says that I should ask him to pray for me and for my forgiveness.
What does that mean? I can make it clearer with an example.

My daughter may fall very ill, God forbid. May Allah protect our children from trials. I give this only as an example to make the point clearer. She becomes very sick and is admitted to the emergency room. The doctors come to me and say that she is in severe pain and cannot breathe properly.

As a father, I cannot even imagine the state I would be in if that ever happened. Nothing is more painful for a parent than seeing his own child suffer, whether the suffering is physical, mental, or spiritual. Then the doctor tells me that she cannot breathe and must be put on a ventilator.

At that moment, there would be no other place in the world where I would want to be. I would not leave my daughter's side even for a second. I would sit beside her because I love her so much. I would remain at her bedside, constantly praying for her.
Then Allah answers my prayers. She wakes up. She says, “Babu! I want ice cream.”

I would be ready at once. “You want ice cream? Of course. What flavor do you want?” If I could not find it there, I would drive wherever I had to drive to get that ice cream for her. That is what I would do.
At that point, I would feel intensely close to her. “What else do you want, sweetheart? Is there anything else I can do for you? Is there anything else I can get for you?”
It so happened that, just before she fell ill, we had a terrible fight. She had disobeyed me and spoken to me very rudely. I was still angry with her when all of this happened.
Then she wakes up and remembers what she did. She says, “Babu, I'm sorry for what I did and said. Please forgive me!”
I know what I would say: “Forgive you? Sweetheart, there's nothing to forgive. I'm not upset with you at all anymore. Don't even think about it.”
That is how parents are with their children. There is nothing strange in it.

If this is how deeply I love my child, then Allah's love for his creation is beyond what I can imagine. According to a HADEES, Allah holds the love of seventy mothers for every single one of his creation. In such an affliction, I felt intensely close to my daughter. When a creation of Allah is going through trials and afflictions, Allah is nearer to him than I can grasp.

I was ready to respond to anything my daughter asked for in that moment, though my ability is extremely limited. But when a human being, a creation of Allah , is in pain and asks for something, whether for himself or for someone else, Allah does not refuse him in that moment.

When I am afflicted, Allah is closest to me in that very moment, closer than any human being could ever be. When I turn to Allah for forgiveness with true repentance, there is nothing He would not forgive, whatever sin I may have committed and however terribly I may have behaved. Allah would forgive instantly.

I do not hesitate for a second to forgive my child. The mercy of Allah is far greater. He is the One who makes Himself known through love. He holds the love of seventy mothers for His creation, so He does not refuse forgiveness.

If I were angry with my son, and my daughter woke up and said to me, “Babu! Please forgive my brother,” would I refuse? “Oh my God, you are in such a difficult state. You are in so much pain. You are suffering so much right now, and even in this state you are concerned about your brother? You want me to forgive him? Your request will surely be granted. Of course I forgive him. I will give you anything you want right now. All you have to do is ask.” SubhanAllah

I can now appreciate the beauty of that HADEES. In the very middle of my affliction, I raise my hands and ask Allah to fulfill another person's need. I now turn from to , which means a slave. Many Muslims feel uneasy with the word slave because it brings a harsh image to mind. Freedom of choice

I begin with the word slave. What is the defining mark of a slave? A slave is someone whose free will has been taken away. He has no choice in the decisions his master makes. He must obey the master's will without question. He has no independent existence except to serve the master's desires.

In worldly slavery, the master denies the slave's freedom and forbids him to choose for himself. That is the deepest humiliation. To take away the freedom of choice from an intelligent human being is to say, “I do not think you are capable of making the right choices.” It is to say, “You are no different from an animal to me. Just as I choose for my cattle and my dog, I will choose for you.” Denying a human being the freedom to choose is the height of humiliation and disgrace.
When I speak of our Master, I ask what the most precious gift is that He gave us. What is the final gift that sets us apart from every other creation in this world? It is free will.

Did He need to give it to us? No. He is . He is my owner. He owns every created thing in this universe. That alone makes every creation His property and His slave. Being His property, or being His slave, therefore has nothing to do with being Muslim or not. Everything belongs to Him. Everything is His slave.
The sun is His property. The moon is His property. The galaxies are His property. This whole universe, and everything within it, including me, belongs to Him.
Does the sun have free will? Does the moon have free will? Do night and day have free will? No. They are all in complete submission to the will of their Creator.
They are all floating in their orbits. They have been bound by gravity. They have no choice except to float where they have been placed. Allah bound them and took away their freedom of choice.

Could He have done that to us? Could Allah have bound us? Could He have forced us into submission? The One who compelled and enslaved the sun, the moon, the solar systems, and the galaxies could certainly have forced us into submission.
But did He? No. He gave us intellect and freedom of choice, something He did not give to any other creation. SubhanAllah.

I see from the outset that Allah is truly my master. He is my , but His is unlike the mastery of any other master I know. Every worldly master first tries to take away freedom of choice. Teachers, parents, employers, courts, doctors: any worldly comes with some form of control, some restriction on the will.

Allah alone is the who has granted complete freedom of choice. If denying freedom of choice is the deepest humiliation, then granting full freedom of choice is the highest honor. SubhanAllah. Allah honored us above every other creation by giving us the freedom to choose.
And say: "The truth has been revealed by your master." Then whosoever wills, let him believe, and whosoever wills, let him disbelieve

Every master I know gives the minimum and demands the maximum from his slaves.

Among all created beings, our master has given us the most. The rest of creation remains constantly in to him. They work around the clock, in constant obedience to Allah, without a moment's break, in order to serve us.
Yet although he has given us the most, he asks the least from us in return:
one hour of each day; one month of fasting out of twelve, and even that only from sunrise to sunset; 2.5% of our wealth in , from wealth he gave us in the first place.

This is astonishing. How easy has he made it for us? What kind of master does this? I know of no other master in this world who makes matters so easy for a slave. I know of no other master who gives so much and asks for so little in return. Such a master is unheard of.
Explanations

And if that generosity were not enough, he also sent revelation and messengers to explain his reasons to us. Does a master ever explain his reasons to his slaves?
