Allah desires ease for you. He does not desire hardship for you.
Who does it benefit?
I ask another question. Who are the acts of worship meant to benefit: Him or us? In every ordinary master-slave relationship, slavery is arranged for the master's benefit, not the slave's.

But this Master designed the universe for us. He gave us the most and asked the least in return. He even explained the reasons behind His commands. So the question becomes: everything He has asked us to do, whom does it benefit? It benefits us, and only us. SubhanAllah.

Every slave in the world is bought and put to work for the master's gain. Every command given to a slave serves the master's interest. What kind of Master is this, whose every command is for the benefit of His slaves? Not a single command is for His own benefit. If that is not love, if that is not care, if that is not mercy, if that is not ease, if that is not , then what is it? AllahuAkbar.
He is constantly serving us. And what He asks from us in return is also only for our benefit, not His.
Judgment

I ask another question. Is a slave's work judged according to the slave's abilities, or according to the master's expectations? In ordinary slavery, a slave's work is judged by the master's standards and demands.

If Our Relationship With Allah Is Of Master And Slave, Then What Is The Concept Of Freedom In Islam?

What is freedom? . In Arabic, freedom is very different from the way modern English usually defines it. In pre-Islamic Arab culture, the stood in contrast to the slave. A free person was someone who was not a . Such a person possessed both and .

Fear Of Punishment

The first is fear of punishment in this world. This is a worldly form of retribution, called . Human nature fears pain. In fact, fear of pain is often a stronger immediate force than the desire for pleasure. When two choices stand before a person, and either outcome seems equally possible, the person will usually choose avoiding pain over gaining pleasure.

I remember a study done in the United States, I think over 30 years. It was a very interesting study. Researchers took five-year-old children and offered each of them a cookie. They said, “you can have this cookie right now or if you wait 10 minutes you can have two cookies.” The children made very different choices.

The researchers then followed these children over 30 years. They found, almost consistently, that the children who delayed gratification for a greater reward became far more successful in life than those who wanted the reward immediately. The study was striking because it showed how important delayed gratification is: accepting a temporary deprivation in the hope of something greater.

A central teaching of Islam, and of the Abrahamic traditions more broadly, is that reality has both physics and metaphysics. Physical laws can be known from the world that is touched and felt. This world has cause and effect. An action produces a reaction. If I strike a table, a sound follows. If no sound follows, then some physical law appears to have been suspended, and the matter would need investigation, because by the laws of physics the strike should produce sound. If a person jumps from a building, that cause has an effect.

In the same way, there are metaphysical laws. Cause and effect are not limited to the physical world. They extend into the spiritual world, and also into the inner world of the self. If I shout at someone, there is an inward effect. The emotions themselves are not fully understood, because they belong to consciousness. Yet when I shout, something is felt inside. Depression may arise, or anger may arise. That belongs to another realm. It is not merely physical. It is the realm of the emotions.
So just as actions have physical effects, they also have spiritual effects.

I take, for instance, the Arabic expression , which literally means “water of the face.” The meaning is the purity, or impurity, that appears on a person's face. When people sin repeatedly, their evil begins to show in their faces. A kind of metaphysical darkness settles there. In the same way, people who do many good deeds are also marked by them. A light, or brightness, appears on the face.

The Arabs used to call the face , meaning “the register,” because it records everything. Someone once said that by fifty, everyone has the face he deserves. By that age, a life has made itself visible. If the life has been good, it shows on the face. Fear of otherworldly punishment, then, is one of the things that moves a person to do good and remain within proper limits.

The next motivating factor for is the desire for benefit. Human beings also want what benefits them. At the most basic level, this is the principle of stick and carrot. The highest people, and the most intelligent, rise beyond stick and carrot. They move into another realm. Maulana Ali often said in his prayers:

This is a very high station of worship. It rises completely beyond the philosophy of carrot and stick. Yet most people remain at that basic level. Because the Quran speaks to all humanity, it often speaks in this general way.

The prophet said: move according to the level of the least among you. The whole community therefore moves with the weakest within it. It does not rush ahead and leave people behind. That is the way of Islam. A careful study of this religion shows that much of it is designed to protect the weakest people.

Some people can stand on their own without difficulty. Others cannot, because they carry ordinary human weaknesses. The protects such people. This is why the Quran speaks against things such as gambling. The Quran says that there is some good in gambling:
They ask you concerning alcohol and gambling. Tell them: "In them is a great sin, and also benefit for men, but their sin is far greater than their benefit."

I understand the Quran to be saying that gambling contains some benefit. There are lessons to be learned from it. Risk itself is an important feature of commerce, and gambling has a close relationship with commerce. Yet the harms of gambling are far greater than its benefits.

It is a known fact in the social sciences that about three percent of people who enter a gambling casino become addicted. Gambling destroys their lives. I went inside a casino in Atlantic City many years ago, and it was one of the most frightening things I had ever seen. It felt like a circle from Dante's Inferno. Gambling works through the carrot. It is a carrot phenomenon. The gambler thinks, “If I put the money in and pull the lever, I may win.” The whole system is designed so that winning happens just often enough to keep a person there. When people leave, they say, “I made such and such.” They do not say how much they lost. They always speak of what they won.

That is the phenomenon of the carrot. It is used often, and it is one of the worst things about gambling. In worldly pleasures, what gives pleasure is usually followed by a far greater pain. That is simply how it is designed.

A familiar example appears in business. A company often conducts internal audits, especially in countries such as the United States or England, where revenue agencies may examine its records. I take another benefit of this verse, , to be that it creates shame, or modesty, born from awareness of God. Allah is aware of human actions. Allah is watching. That awareness should produce shame and modesty before Him.

Anthropologists often divide cultures into two broad types: shame cultures and guilt cultures. Western cultures usually fall under the second type.

A guilt culture builds moral restraints inside a person. When people raised in such a culture do something wrong, they feel pain within themselves. Many observers have noted that people in the West often find it difficult to commit wrong actions without feeling bad afterward.

In America, an entire industry has grown around helping people overcome guilt. Self-help books and self-improvement courses often draw on this need. In guilt cultures, then, the main restraining mechanism is internal.

I find the restraining mechanisms in shame cultures to be external. People avoid wrong actions because they fear other people. That fear may restrain behavior, but it often produces hypocrisy, because the restraint does not live inside the person.

India, Pakistan, and many other Asian countries are deeply shaped by shame culture. In such societies, many people are controlled mainly by outside pressure. When a person remains in his own country, certain acts feel shameful. When he goes to another country, the same acts may no longer feel shameful, so he may begin doing them without feeling any inward pain.

This explains why many young people from India and Pakistan, when they come to the United States or to the West, lose all restraint. They may drink, party, and take drugs, though they never did these things at home. The acts become socially possible because they are no longer living inside the culture that made those acts shameful.

A different country also gives a person anonymity. At home, everyone knows him. They know his parents. If he does anything, the whole community may hear about it. In another city or another country, that social net is gone. Shame becomes harder to feel.

For this reason, guilt cultures are very important in advanced societies. Shame works well at the tribal level and in small communities. Once life moves into large and advanced societies, shame begins to break down.

Islam is rooted in a shame culture, but it lifts shame beyond human society and grounds it in shame before God. The force is not only inward. It is also external, because it is tied to modesty, to before God and before His angels.

I know a very interesting story. More than a hundred years ago, when the British ruled India, there lived a pickpocket. He was Muslim, but he earned his living by stealing from people's pockets. He belonged to a gang that did the same work.

The self has already received close attention, as has the theme of the Quran. What opens now is a new group of topics, gathered under the heading "Know Thy Master." Within this group, the focus falls on Allah — His various attributes, His relationship with us, and what He expects of us. The ground to be covered includes His proof of existence, His mercy, and the matter of fate and destiny.

Any serious discussion of Allah begins with the word , because the name Allah grows from the root . To grasp the depth of that root, however, requires first understanding the Quranic concept of love: . The Islamic conception of love differs sharply from what Bollywood and Hollywood offer under that name. Understanding therefore demands a clear account of love — and understanding love, in turn, demands starting with friendship. Love always begins there. No genuine love for a person takes root until friendship with that person has first been established. Real friendship, when it deepens, flowers into pure love.

Lust needs no friendship. This is why one-night stands and casual, meaningless sex spread through society — they are rooted in lust, in the base animal instinct of studied earlier. Animals do not need to become friends before they mate. Love, however, always begins in the sentiments of friendship. The Arabs say that whenever the plant of love grows, it grows in the soil of friendship. Before turning to the term , then, the various shades of love must first be laid out — and before that, the different types of friendship the Quran speaks of must be understood.

In the present age, genuine friendship has grown extraordinarily difficult to form. The world has moved toward virtual connections — the kind sustained by social media platforms and electronic devices. Human beings have grown so enslaved to their phones that a simple fifteen-minute conversation between two people, uninterrupted by the pull of a screen, has become nearly impossible. The more tightly connected people have become to their devices, the more disconnected they have become from one another. Real, unhurried conversation between human beings has all but vanished. Instead of owning these devices, people are owned by them. The device has become the master; its user, the obedient slave. The moment it sounds, everything else is dropped and attention snaps to the screen in total submission — — I hear and I obey.

The parallel is almost comic. People with asthma reach for an inhaler every few minutes because they cannot breathe. Phones have made us the same way. The frantic search for a signal — the inability to simply sit without one — has become its own kind of respiratory crisis. Not long ago, I was telling my daughter about the and about going for . I asked her what she would like to know about Mecca. The first thing she asked was whether they have Wi-Fi there. As sad as it is, that is what life has been reduced to.
The Quranic concept of friendship, then, deserves serious attention — and the angle from which it is approached makes all the difference. There are two ways to enter this subject:
The first is to ask what kind of friends one should look for. The second is to ask what kind of friend one should be to others.

The first approach is the selfish one, and the Quran does not endorse it. The correct approach is the second: not what kind of friends to have, but what kind of friend to be. The distinction matters enormously. When a person becomes the right kind of friend to others, Allah places the right kind of people in that person's path.

The Quran uses at least ten distinct words for friendship, each carrying its own shade of meaning and appearing in contexts that illuminate something specific about the relationship. Moving through some of these terms reveals what Allah is teaching about the different kinds of bonds between people.
Protective Friend

The first term is . It derives from , which conveys the idea of protection. A is someone who manages another's affairs and always has that person's back. When trouble strikes — of any kind — the is there to guard and shield. He does not merely help after the fact; he handles the situation entirely. A therefore denotes not friendship in a general sense but something stronger: a dependable ally who can be counted on both to pull someone out of a crisis and to keep that person from falling into one in the first place. One of the names of Allah is .

Allah is the Wali of those who believe. He brings them out from darkness into light. But as for those who disbelieve, their Auliya are Taghut , they bring them out from light into darkness. Those are the dwellers of the Fire, and they will abide therein forever.
Allah is the of those who believe. He is a protective friend to those who believe.

A related form of this same root is the word . It describes that same caring, concerned friend who also holds the ability to protect — specifically when he takes on a position of authority. The idea is this: when someone is entirely convinced that another person truly cares for them, truly has their best interests at heart, and they simply submit to that person's authority and heed what he says, that person will protect them from trouble, or help them out of it when they are already in it. The one who stands in that position of authority over their affairs is called .

This is precisely why the phrase carries such weight. The word is used there not only to affirm his authority over our affairs, but, more fundamentally, to establish that he is our caring and concerned friend — the one who is there to protect us, whose teachings exist to protect us and keep us from harm. He is someone who always has our back; his teachings always have our best interests at heart. By placing the word before his name, the testimony affirms his — his genuine, sincere love, care, and concern for us — precisely in order to protect us.

Unhealthy Shame

I think one problem with Islamic training today is that many of us are raised without solid roots. The method becomes a rule-and-shame method. From childhood, the main lesson is often and hellfire. The emphasis falls here: if a person does , that person will enter Hellfire.

That is how many of us were raised, and it is also how many of us raise our children. It is true that certain things are . It is true that hellfire exists. It is true that Allah has anger and wrath. All of this is true.

But the problem is one of emphasis. Why are children taught these realities above Allah's mercy? Why are they not taught that Allah is the most merciful, and that even after a mistake, a person can repent and begin again? Why is that not the message placed before them?
Unfortunately, the answer is that fear becomes a way to control the child's behavior. Many of us use fear as the tool of control. The problem is that it backfires.
I have seen how it backfires. When false fear, false shame, or unhealthy shame is used to control a person's behavior, it does not build solid roots. It builds avoidance.

A child may grow up in a home where the warning is constant: "You better watch out, or the police are going to throw you in jail. You better not make a mistake. You better not do this; you better not do that." In effect, the child is taught to fear the police. The police are presented as a wrathful and frightening power.

With that kind of training, the best outcome is that the child learns to avoid the police. But closeness does not grow from avoidance. Trust does not grow from fear. The child will not want friendship with the police, will not confide problems to them, and will not ask them for help when trouble comes. The reason is simple: the police have been described only as punishers, so the child does not trust them.

This kind of training does not build in our youth, nor does it build it in us. It builds avoidance. Many people raised this way grow up wanting nothing to do with Allah . They want to avoid Allah and religion.

Their reasoning is painful but plain: everything is , and no matter what they do, they believe they will end up in hell. If everything is wrong, then effort feels pointless. If one small mistake means punishment from Allah, then the safest path seems to be avoiding the whole matter of Allah and avoiding religion altogether.

The result has backfired. I am trying to grow the tree of Islam within myself and within my children, but without a solid foundation that tree cannot stand. Even if such an Islam were to grow by some miracle, it would not survive the smallest earthquake.

I need to focus on building a solid foundation. Life will strike, and I will be shaken. The age itself shows this clearly, with temptations all around us. The tree of Islam within our hearts will be shaken from time to time by tests and trials. Allah says in the Quran
Or think you that you will enter Paradise without such as came to those who passed away before you?

They were afflicted with severe poverty and illness, and they were shaken so deeply that even the Messenger and those who believed with him said, "When the Help of Allah?" Yes, certainly, the Help of Allah is near.
Entry into Paradise is not attained without passing through what those before us passed through.
They were struck by calamity, hardship, and struggle, and they were shaken. The Arabic word comes from the same root as , which means earthquake.
I see that they were shaken so severely that even the messengers, together with those who believed with them, asked when the Help of Allah would come. And Allah says:

Indeed, the Help of Allah is near. The Help of Allah is not merely present as an idea. It is present now, with me, while I am passing through the test. Allah says that He is closer to us than our jugular vein.

I will be shaken from time to time. The question is how a building survives an earthquake. The answer returns to its foundation, because the foundation determines its . So I must ask myself what kind of foundation I have with Allah . When I am tested through pain or through pleasure, will I remain firm on the straight path? If the answer is no, then I need to work on my relationship with Allah, not merely on the rules.

This is why the scholars said that the first verses revealed did not begin by commanding people to give up alcohol and fornication. If revelation had begun there, people would have said that they would never give those things up. The reason is that the foundation had not yet been built. The roots of the tree had not yet taken hold. When a person is given rules at the very beginning, those rules will not be followed if they stand against what that person wants.
We are making this mistake often. We are not building a foundation. Instead, we keep throwing rules at children.

We are not helping them form an attachment to Allah. We are not teaching them to love Allah. We are not teaching them what it truly means to rely on Allah. That foundation is barely being taught. What children often receive instead is a list of rulings:
It is to eat this. It is to drink this. It is to dress like this. It is to say this.
That is all. The problem with this method is that it is being rejected.

The scholar's point was exactly this: if the rules had come first, even the Companions would have rejected them. If Allah had begun with commands and prohibitions before building the foundation, they would not have been ready to carry them. But Allah did not begin with rules.

, the thirtieth chapter of the Quran, is mostly Meccan. Most of the verses in that were revealed at the beginning of Islam. It contains very few legal rulings. Instead, it speaks about Allah, His love, His mercy, and the Day of Judgment. It speaks about human beings and their relationship with Allah. It speaks about the human soul. It speaks about , , and retribution. It teaches . It focuses on how people should treat one another. That is what stands in , because that was the work of building the foundation.
If we want , we have to build a foundation rooted in the love of Allah.

I have generally spoken about in terms of shame and fear. Fear itself is not always blameworthy. Psychology also distinguishes between healthy fear and unhealthy fear, and that distinction matters here.

When a person does something deeply wrong and becomes afraid that parents or loved ones will find out, that fear can move in two directions. Sometimes it makes him go back to the people he has hurt. At other times, it makes him run away and hide.

There are, in essence, two ways to respond after harming someone or making a mistake. If a person hurts his closest friend or his spouse, shame may become so heavy that he hides. He avoids the person. He avoids the issue. He avoids the conversation. He creates distance from the very relationship that needs repair. That is not a healthy response. It does not solve the problem; it makes it worse.

The same pattern appears in the relationship with Allah. Many people make a mistake and feel ashamed. But instead of turning back to Allah, they run away from Allah. They try to hide from Him. Prayer begins to feel unbearable because shame stands in the way. Speaking about Allah becomes difficult. In some cases, a person may even want to leave religion altogether, not because the truth has disappeared, but because shame has become too painful to face.

But there is a healthier way to deal with that harm. When I have wronged someone, the healthiest repair is to go to that person and apologize: to say that I am sorry, that I regret what I did, that I admit I made a mistake, and that I will try to do better.

That is and . That is what I am supposed to do. It is healthy fear. It is a healthy response to a mistake. Instead of hiding from Allah, instead of saying that I want nothing to do with religion or nothing to do with God, instead of giving up and refusing to pray because I have committed so many sins and feel too ashamed to face Allah, I return.

That kind of shame, when it drives a person away from Allah, is unhealthy. But is healthy fear. It is the kind of healthy shame that helps me stay away from what displeases Allah and angers Him. And when I do what angers Allah, it makes me rush to apologize, rush to repent, show my regret, and try to make things right.

I mention this because I feel that we are feeding the wrong kind of fear and shame. When Allah is taught as though He were a frightening policeman, , people are trained to avoid Him. A person trains himself, his children, and those around him to run away from Allah instead of running toward Him: to apologize, repent, and repair what has been broken.

I need healthy fear because it draws me closer to Allah and moves me to repent. Unhealthy shame does the opposite: it makes me run away from Allah and avoid Him out of shame. For me to remain firm in my and to have , I need to develop this healthy fear of Allah , called .
Myth of Perfection

Healthy fear has a seed. Healthy begins from something small, and unhealthy shame also begins from a seed. A seed grows into a tree, but the whole tree begins at that first point. Anything that grows must be understood at its root.

The seed of unhealthy shame is the belief that I am supposed to be perfect. This myth of perfection lies at the root of many of our problems. It may be taught to me, or I may come to believe it myself: that I am actually meant to be flawless. Once I believe that, every mistake becomes a reason for unhealthy shame.
The inner response becomes simple and painful: I was supposed to be perfect, but I am not perfect, so I am ashamed of myself. I stop trying. That shame leads me toward despair.
The root cause was not the mistake itself. The seed was the false belief that I was supposed to be perfect, a belief often handed down by family and teachers.

The root of healthy , healthy , and healthy is the return to Allah. That root is the knowledge that every human being will make mistakes. It is the opposite of the myth of perfection. It is the realization that the human being is imperfect, and that we have been created as imperfect human beings.

When I know this and understand it, I respond with repentance. I know that I am human, and that I have fallen into error. So I try to repair what I have done. I try to repent. I try again. Even if I make the same mistake again and again, I do not give up trying to become better. That is the essence of .
The prophet said
, All children of Adam will make mistakes; and the best of them are the ones who repent

I have to let go of the myth of perfection, because it lies at the root of many of my problems. It is one reason I keep falling into despair. If I am told that I am supposed to be perfect, and then I discover that I am not perfect, the result is frustration.

But when I understand that human beings are imperfect by design, the matter changes. No one can go against the divine design. Allah said that He created human beings imperfect. The descriptions in the Quran about our creation show this clearly.

These descriptions are not outside the human being: weak, created from a filthy liquid, hasty, anxious. I cannot go against that design. It is impossible. When I try to fight what Allah has placed in human nature, I end by striking against despair. Then Allah balances these weaknesses by telling us

Say, "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves [by sinning], do not despair of the mercy of Allah . Indeed, Allah forgives all sins. Indeed, it is He who is the Forgiving, the Merciful."

Allah tells them: O My beloved servants who have wronged their own selves. When I commit sin, I do not harm Allah. I harm only myself. I cannot wrong Allah, take anything from Him, or lessen His kingdom. Allah's kingdom is infinite.

Wrongdoing and forbidden acts wound my own soul. The example is simple: if I drink poison, I harm myself, not the doctor. If I refuse the medicine, I harm myself, not the doctor. In the same way, Allah is not the One I wrong. I am the one I wrong. So Allah says
“O My servant who has done wrong, who has transgressed against his own soul.
Do not despair of the mercy of Allah.”

Allah tells me not to despair. Yet despair often enters because the soul carries a false idea of itself and a false idea of Allah. I imagine that I am meant to be perfect, and that I must be perfect. Then, if I am not perfect, I see myself as worthless.
That is an all-or-nothing way of seeing the self:
either an angel, or a devil; either pure white, or pure black.

That false measure must fall away. is not one or the other. is not an angel, and he is not a devil. A believer is flawed, but he continually strives to repent and tries hard to set himself right. He keeps rising after he falls. He does not give up.

This is why the Prophet said that all the children of Adam make mistakes, and the best of those who make mistakes are those who repent. When I let go of the false demand for perfection, I become able to rise again after I fall.

I have also learned something counter-intuitive: feeds on this false sense of perfection. He turns it into a weapon against me. When I make a mistake, he comes and says, “Look at you! How shameful you are! Are you going to pray now, after doing this? You are such a terrible person. You are nothing but a hypocrite. Look at you! Are you going to stand before Allah now after doing this? He is not even going to look at you. Do you think you deserve his mercy? Do you think you deserve his love?”

This is how uses false perfection against me. First he pushes me into unhealthy shame. He drags my face through it. Then, after I have finished shaming myself and beating myself down, he comes again and says, “Do you really want to believe in a God who puts you through this mental torture? Think about it! Allah created you imperfect and is now demanding perfection from you? What a horrible master!”

This is how works. He is the one who pushed me into unhealthy shame, and then he comes from another direction: “How could Allah do this to you? How could he put that alcohol in your presence? Did he not know you are weak? Did he not know you would drink it? Why would he do that to you? Does this whole religion not seem stupid?”
And then I say, “Screw religion!”

But when I realize that I am not perfect, and that I was never created to be perfect, then when comes at me in that way, I can say, “Yes, I made a mistake. But my Allah is the Most Merciful. My Allah is the Most Forgiving. He will forgive me if I try again. Even if I fail again and repent, He will forgive me again. I will keep trying until I get it right.”
That is what Allah wants me to have: hope in His mercy.

I heard the Messenger of Allah (?) say: Allah the Almighty said: O son of Adam, as long as you call upon Me and ask from Me, I shall forgive you for what you have done, and I shall not mind. O son of Adam, if your sins were to reach the clouds of the sky, and then you asked Me for forgiveness, I would forgive you. O son of Adam, if you came to Me with sins nearly as great as the earth, and then met Me without ascribing any partner to Me, I would bring you forgiveness nearly as great as it.

I understand from this HADEES that Allah says: if a person comes to Allah with sins that fill the whole space between the heavens and the earth, and then sincerely repents to Allah, Allah will grant forgiveness as vast as that, or even greater.

That is who Allah is. Allah is not like a policeman waiting to throw people into jail. Allah is the Most Merciful. The problem is that we are not teaching his mercy. We are teaching only his wrath. We are not teaching attachment to Allah; we are teaching only rules. We are not speaking about the roots. We are fighting over the leaves.
The whole concern becomes outward form:
Eat like this. Dress like this. Walk like this. Eat, sleep, and spit like this. This is allowed, and this is not allowed. These ingredients in food are really , and those are not really, really .
I have even seen a bottle of water labeled “Halal certified.” It was water.

This is missing the forest for the trees. More than that, it is missing the forest for a single leaf on the trees. We are not focusing on the roots. The result is one of two things: either an aversion to religion that turns into hatred and complete abandonment, or an external shell of that falls apart at the first wind of trial.

I do not belittle the importance of outward worship. As I said at the beginning, our includes both outward worship and inward worship. That is why I began there. It is both and . My point is that one cannot be taken while the other is left behind.

The problem is that many of us focus only on the outward form. When worship is reduced to its outer shape, it becomes like a tree grown without roots, or a building raised without a foundation. When the wind comes, the tree falls. When an earthquake comes, the building collapses. Solid roots are necessary.
Practical Foundation Building

The practical question, then, is how those solid roots are built. First, the myth of human perfection has to be removed. A different understanding must take its place: the human being was not created to be perfect. The human being was created to keep repenting and keep trying again.
A child learning to walk does not fall once and then abandon walking forever. If that were the rule, the child would simply sit there, and walking would end before it began.

The same is true of a person driving. A wrong turn does not mean the engine must be switched off, the car put in park, and the journey abandoned: "I'm done - that's it! I made a wrong turn." Even the GPS does not speak that way. It does not say, "You made a wrong turn - sorry! Just stop trying and turn off the car. Your trip is over!" It says something else: "Recalculating." "Rerouting."

That is . It is, quite literally, , because means to return: re-turn. is the inward mechanism that reroutes the servant back to Allah. That is the process of . In Arabic, the word literally means to turn around and return.

A car's GPS can reroute again and again. It does not stop after one wrong turn. Even after several wrong turns, it does not say, "You're an idiot! Its pointless trying to give you directions, you keep making the wrong turns. I'm not going to guide you anymore." It continues to reroute, as many times as needed. A GPS can do that. Allah can do far more. SubhanAllah.
My way of thinking has to change. Falling is not the end. The servant gets back up, repents, keeps going, and tries again. That is the first foundation of .
I can develop this foundation in a very simple way. It is a recipe with three ingredients.

This is like oxygen for the heart. It keeps a person alive spiritually, psychologically, and mentally. No matter what happens, even if the worst sins have been committed, prayer must not be ignored. If five prayers feel beyond reach, I begin with what I can. At the very least, I try to pray once a day.

I should rejoice in that prayer. I should feel glad and grateful for it, even if it seemed distracted or imperfect. The myth of perfection creates a serious problem. If I asked a person to list every sin and mistake committed in one day, the list would probably be long. If I asked for the good deeds of that same day, the list would be harder to make. That is because the wrong is often beaten into the soul, while the good is not appreciated with the same force.

From now on, every good deed deserves attention. After doing good, I remember Allah, feel grateful to him, and praise him by saying . I keep bringing Allah to mind after every good deed, and I allow myself to feel glad about it: from remembering to say before eating, to saving someone's life, and everything between those two. My relationship with Allah grows when I think of him and consciously realize that every good act pleases him.
This is the daily , the remembrance of Allah through supplications. It is the GPS that keeps rerouting the servant.
3. The recitation and understanding of Quran
I have to stay connected to the Quran every day, even if only briefly, even if only one verse a day. When this connection is daily and consistent, it builds : resilience on the straight path, the .
